Most of these particles can be detected by the particle detector surrounding the collision point. For example, quarks undergo a process called

in which they become a shower of subatomic particles, called "jet''. In addition, the high magnetic field present in the detectors allows even very energetic charged particles to curve enough for their momentum to be determined. The ATLAS detector uses a superconducting solenoid system that produces a constant and uniform 2.00 Tesla magnetic field in the inner part of the detector, surrounding the collision point. Charged particles with momenta below a certain value will be curved so strongly that they will loop repeatedly in the field and most likely not be measured. Due to its nature, the neutrino is not detected at all, as it escapes through the detector without interacting.

Where is the neutrino? (10 points)


When two protons collide with a very high energy at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), several particles may be produced as a result of that collision, such as electrons, muons, neutrinos, quarks, and their respective anti-particles. Most of these particles can be detected by the particle detector surrounding the collision point. For example, quarks undergo a process called 
hadronisation
 in which they become a shower of subatomic particles, called "jet''. In addition, the high magnetic field present in the detectors allows even very energetic charged particles to curve enough for their momentum to be determined. The ATLAS detector uses a superconducting solenoid system that produces a constant and uniform 2.00 Tesla magnetic field in the inner part of the detector, surrounding the collision point. Charged particles with momenta below a certain value will be curved so strongly that they will loop repeatedly in the field and most likely not be measured. Due to its nature, the neutrino is not detected at all, as it escapes through the detector without interacting.

solution.text:
Where is the neutrino? (10 points)


Part A. ATLAS Detector physics (4.0 points)


A.1


The magnetic force is the centripetal force: 
\[\begin{equation*}
m\frac{v^2}{r} = evB \Rightarrow r = \frac{mv}{eB} \; .
\end{equation*}\]
 First express the velocity in terms of the kinetic energy, 
\[\begin{equation*}
K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{2K}{m}} \; ,
\end{equation*}\]
 and then insert it in the expression above for the radius to get


A.1
0.5pt


\[r = \frac{\sqrt{2Km}}{eB} \; .\]


A.2


The radius of the circular motion of a charged particle in the presence of a uniform magnetic field is given by, 
\[\begin{equation*}
r = \frac{mv}{eB} \; .
\end{equation*}\]
 This formula is valid in the relativistic scenario if the mass correction, 
\(m \to \gamma m\)
 is included: 
\[\begin{equation*}
r = \frac{\gamma mv}{eB} = \frac{p}{eB} \Rightarrow p = reB \; .
\end{equation*}\]
 Note that the radius of the circular motion is half the radius of the inner part of the detector. One obtains [1 MeV/
\(c = 5.34 \times 10^{-22}\)
 m kg s
\(^{-1}\)
]


A.2
0.5pt


\[p = 330 \; \mathrm{MeV}/c \; .\]


A.3


The acceleration for the particle is 
\(a = \frac{evB}{\gamma m} \sim \frac{ecB}{\gamma m}\)
, in the ultrarelativistic limit. Then, 
\[\begin{equation*}
P = \frac{e^4c^2\gamma^4B^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0c^3\gamma^2m^2} = \frac{e^4\gamma^2c^4B^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0c^5m^2} \; .
\end{equation*}\]
 Since 
\(E = \gamma mc^2\)
 we can obtain 
\(\gamma^2c^4 = \frac{E^2}{m^2}\)
 and, finally, 
\[P = \frac{e^4}{6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5}E^2B^2 \; .\]
 Therefore,


A.3
1.0pt


\[\xi = \frac{1}{6\pi} \; , \quad n = 5 \text{ and } k = 4 \; .\]


A.4


The power emitted by the particle is given by, 
\[P = -\frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{e^4}{6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5}E^2B^2 \; .\]
 The energy of the particle as a function of time can be calculated from 
\[\int_{E_0}^{E(t)} \frac{1}{E^2}\,\mathrm{d}E = -\int_0^t \frac{e^4}{6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5}B^2\,\mathrm{d}t \; ,\]
 where 
\(E(0) = E_0\)
. This leads to, 
\[\frac{1}{E(t)} - \frac{1}{E_0} = \frac{e^4B^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5}\, t \quad\Rightarrow\quad E(t) = \frac{E_0}{1 + \alpha E_0 t} \; ,\]
 with


A.4
1.0pt


\[\alpha = \frac{e^4B^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5} \; .\]


A.5


If the initial energy of the electron is 100 GeV, the radius of curvature is extremely large (
\(r = \frac{E}{eBc} \approx 167\)
 m). Therefore, in approximation, one can consider the electron is moving in the inner part of the ATLAS detector along a straight line. The time of flight of the electron is 
\(t = R/c\)
, where 
\(R = 1.1\)
 m is the radius of the inner part of the detector. The total energy lost due to synchrotron radiation is, 
\[\Delta E = E(R/c) - E_0 = \frac{E_0}{1 + \alpha E_0 \frac{R}{c}} - E_0 \approx -\alpha E_0^2 \frac{R}{c}\]
 and


A.5
0.5pt


\[\Delta E = -56 \; \mathrm{MeV} \; .\]


A.6


In the ultrarelativistic limit, 
\(v \approx c\)
 and 
\(E \approx pc\)
. The cyclotron frequency is, 
\[\omega(t) = \frac{c}{r(t)} = \frac{ecB}{p(t)} = \frac{ec^2B}{E(t)}\]


A.6
0.5pt


\[\omega(t) = \frac{ec^2B}{E_0}\left(1 + \frac{e^4B^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5}E_0t\right) \; .\]


Part B. Finding the neutrino (6.0 points)


B.1


Since the 
\(W^+\)
 boson decays into an anti-muon and a neutrino, one can use principles of conservation of energy and linear momentum to calculate the unknown 
\(p_z^{(\nu)}\)
 of the neutrino. Moreover, the anti-muon and the neutrino can be considered massless, which implies that the magnitude of their momenta (times 
\(c\)
) and their energies are the same. Therefore, the conservation of linear momentum can be expressed as 
\[\vec{p}^{\,(W)} = \vec{p}^{\,(\mu)} + \vec{p}^{\,(\nu)} \; ,\]
 and the conservation of energy as, 
\[E^{(W)} = cp^{(\mu)} + cp^{(\nu)} \; .\]
 In addition, one can also relate the energy and the momentum of the 
\(W^+\)
 boson through its mass, 
\[m_W^2 = (E^{(W)})^2/c^4 - (p^{(W)})^2/c^2\]
 which leads to a quadratic equation on 
\(p_z^{(\nu)}\)
, 
\[\begin{aligned}
m_W^2 &= \left[(p^{(\mu)} + p^{(\nu)})^2 - (\vec{p}^{\,(\mu)} + \vec{p}^{\,(\nu)})^2\right]/c^2 \\
&= \left(2p^{(\mu)}p^{(\nu)} - 2\vec{p}^{\,(\mu)} \cdot \vec{p}^{\,(\nu)}\right)/c^2
\end{aligned}\]


B.1
1.5pt


\[m_W^2 = \frac{1}{c^2}\left(2p^{(\mu)}\sqrt{(p_{\mathrm{T}}^{(\nu)})^2 + (p_z^{(\nu)})^2} - 2\vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\mu)} \cdot \vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\nu)} - 2p_z^{(\mu)}p_z^{(\nu)}\right) \; .\]


B.2


The numerical substitution directly in the answer of B.1, using 
\[p^{(\mu)} = 37.2\,\mathrm{GeV}/c \quad m_W^2c^2 = 6464.2\,(\mathrm{GeV}/c)^2 \quad (p_{\mathrm{T}}^{(\nu)})^2 = 10\,864.9\,(\mathrm{GeV}/c)^2\]
 
\[\vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\mu)} \cdot \vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\nu)} = 2439.3\,(\mathrm{GeV}/c)^2 \quad p_z^{(\mu)} = -12.4\,\mathrm{GeV}/c \; ,\]
 leads to 
\[6464.2 = 74.4\sqrt{10\,864.9 + (p_z^{(\nu)})^2} - 4878.6 + 24.8p^{(\nu)} \; .\]
 This is a quadratic equation, equivalent to 
\[0.88889\,(p_z^{(\nu)})^2 + 101.64\,p_z^{(\nu)} - 12378 = 0\]
 whose solutions are:


B.2
1.5pt


\[p_z^{(\nu)} = 74.0 \; \mathrm{GeV}/c \quad \text{or} \quad p_z^{(\nu)} = -188.3 \; \mathrm{GeV}/c \; .\]


The general solution of the equation above in B.1 leads to 
\[\begin{aligned}
p_z^{(\nu)} &= \frac{2\vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\mu)} \cdot \vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\nu)}\,p_z^{(\mu)} + m_W^2c^2p_z^{(\mu)}}{2(p_{\mathrm{T}}^{(\mu)})^2} \\
&\pm \frac{p^{(\mu)}\sqrt{-4(p_{\mathrm{T}}^{(\mu)})^2(p_{\mathrm{T}}^{(\nu)})^2 + 4(\vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\mu)} \cdot \vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\nu)})^2 + 4\vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\mu)} \cdot \vec{p}_{\mathrm{T}}^{\,(\nu)}m_W^2c^2 + m_W^4c^4}}{2(p_{\mathrm{T}}^{(\mu)})^2}
\end{aligned}\]
 Numerical substitution leads to the above mentioned values for 
\(p_z^{(\nu)}\)
.


B.3


The final state particles of the top quark decay are the anti-muon, the neutrino and jet 1. Since the neutrino is now fully reconstructed the energy and linear momentum of the top quark can be calculated as, 
\[\begin{aligned}
E^{(\mathrm{t})} &= cp^{(\mu)} + cp^{(\nu)} + cp^{(j_1)} \\
\vec{p}^{\,(\mathrm{t})} &= \vec{p}^{\,(\mu)} + \vec{p}^{\,(\nu)} + \vec{p}^{\,(j_1)} \; .
\end{aligned}\]
 The top quark mass is, 
\[\begin{aligned}
m_{\mathrm{t}} &= \sqrt{(E^{(\mathrm{t})})^2/c^4 - (\vec{p}^{\,(\mathrm{t})})^2/c^2} \\
&= c^{-1}\sqrt{\left(p^{(\mu)} + p^{(\nu)} + p^{(j_1)}\right)^2 - \left(\vec{p}^{\,(\mu)} + \vec{p}^{\,(\nu)} + \vec{p}^{\,(j_1)}\right)^2} \; .
\end{aligned}\]
 The substitution of values leads to two possible masses:

1.0pt


\[m_{\mathrm{t}} = 169.3 \; \mathrm{GeV}/c^2 \quad \text{or} \quad m_{\mathrm{t}} = 311.2 \; \mathrm{GeV}/c^2 \; .\]
